title: Neural embeddings: what the encoder adds
summary: Self-attention is a content addressable lookup with learned, soft matching, which is what gives one vector per word occurrence rather than per word type. It solves the vocabulary problem from Day 3, and costs quadratic attention, larger vectors, and all of your interpretability.
html:
Yesterday your system ranked the right answer fourth because the question said make and the paragraph said ripening. Day 3 named that problem and every day since has failed to solve it. Today you find out what does.

Stop computing the representation. Learn it.

Everything so far derives vectors from counting. TF-IDF is a formula: feed it a corpus, get weights out, and nothing about the procedure ever changes. The dimensions mean something fixed (dimension 4,182 is the word nectar) and the values come from arithmetic you can do by hand.

A neural embedding does not derive the representation. It is a function with a few hundred million learned parameters that maps text to a point in space, and those parameters were fitted so that texts people consider related land near each other. The target is the property you want, rather than a proxy for it.

TF-IDFNeural embedding
Dimensions50,000+ (vocabulary size)384 to 3072, fixed
Non-zero entries~70 out of 50,000all of them
What a dimension meansexactly one wordnothing you can name
Unknown wordsdropped silentlybroken into subwords, still represented
Where values come froma formulafitted parameters

Where the meaning comes from

The training signal rests on an old observation, usually credited to Firth in 1957: you shall know a word by the company it keeps. Words that appear in similar contexts tend to mean similar things.

Nothing tells the model that volume and LUN are the same object. It notices that both are provisioned, mounted, resized, snapshotted and exported, that both sit next to words like array and capacity, and that swapping one for the other rarely changes what the surrounding sentence is doing. Pushed hard enough on enough text, the optimiser has no reason to keep them far apart, and every reason to place them close.

That is the whole answer to Day 3's vocabulary problem. It is not a lookup table of synonyms. It is a side effect of fitting a function to text at scale.

What the encoder adds, specifically

Word2vec did the above in 2013 and it was not enough. It produced one vector per word type, so bank got a single vector that averaged river banks and savings accounts into something that was neither.

A transformer encoder produces one vector per word occurrence, computed from that word's actual neighbours. This is what self-attention is for, and there is a framing that should feel familiar.

Each token emits three projections: a query, a key, and a value. Every token's query is compared against every token's key, the scores are normalised, and each token's new representation becomes a weighted blend of the values it scored highly against.

attention(Q, K, V) = softmax( Q K^T / sqrt(d) ) V

That is a content addressable lookup. Not addressing by position, addressing by what the content is. The difference from a hash table is that the match is soft, every key returns something weighted by relevance rather than one key returning a hit, and the projections that decide what counts as a match are learned rather than specified.

Stack twelve of those layers and bank in "the bank was muddy" ends up somewhere different from bank in "the bank declined it", because at every layer it absorbed a little more of whatever surrounded it. Word order comes back too, via positional encodings added to the inputs, which quietly undoes the bag-of-words loss you accepted on Day 3.

The bill for that

Every token attends to every token, so attention is quadratic in sequence length:

  128 tokens ->      16,384 pairwise scores per head per layer
  512 tokens ->     262,144
 2048 tokens ->   4,194,304
 8192 tokens ->  67,108,864

12 layers x 12 heads: one 512-token chunk costs ~37.7 million attention scores

Going from 512 to 8192 tokens is 16 times the text and 256 times the attention work. That is the real reason max sequence lengths exist, and the reason a model advertising 8192 tokens is not simply a better deal than one at 512.

Storage inverts too, which surprises people:

sparse TF-IDF, ~70 terms      =    560 bytes per chunk
dense  768-dim float32        =  3,072 bytes   (5.5x)
dense 1024-dim float32        =  4,096 bytes   (7.3x)

at 1M chunks:  sparse 0.56 GB   vs   1024-dim dense 4.10 GB

So dense vectors are bigger and they cost more to search, because the inverted-index trick from Day 8 is gone. Every dimension is non-zero, so every chunk has a real score against every query and there is nothing to skip. You are paying more storage and more compute, and what you are buying is that the right answer stops coming fourth. Days 15 to 30 are about making that affordable, and Day 27 is where the 4.10 GB starts shrinking.

What you give up

Interpretability, completely. On Day 8 you could print a query vector, see {"of": 1.0}, and know exactly why the system did something stupid. Print a dense vector and you get 768 floats that mean nothing individually. No dimension is nectar. There is no dimension you can point at.

Debugging changes character as a result. You stop reasoning about why a score came out the way it did and start measuring whether outcomes improved across a set of questions. That is not a minor inconvenience, and it is the honest reason Phase 4 exists as fifteen days rather than a footnote: once your representation is opaque, measurement is the only instrument you have left.

Two more honest limits. Embeddings are still bad at exact identifiers, error codes and part numbers, because a rare string that appeared a handful of times in training has a poorly fitted vector. Day 32 covers that, and Day 33 covers running both systems together rather than choosing. And a model is fitted to whatever text it was trained on, so a corpus full of in-house jargon is outside that distribution and quality drops accordingly.

The encoder hands you one vector per token, and you need one per chunk. How you collapse a few hundred vectors into one is tomorrow: pooling, mean versus CLS, and why the choice matters more than it looks.
exercise:
1. Run the pair you saved on Day 3. You wrote down two sentences and predicted a count based scorer would miss the connection. Install sentence-transformers, load a small model like all-MiniLM-L6-v2, embed both sentences, and compute the cosine. Compare against what your Day 8 scorer gives the same pair. This is the single measurement that shows you what you just bought.

2. Fix failure two. Take the honey question from yesterday and the five chunks. Embed all of them with the same model and rank by cosine. Does the ripening chunk rise? Note that it will not always, and where it does not, you have found something real to keep for Day 12.

3. Test the identifier weakness. Pick an error code or part number from your own systems that appears in your documents. Score a query containing it with both your Day 8 TF-IDF scorer and the neural model. TF-IDF will usually win. That result is the entire argument for hybrid retrieval on Day 33, in your own data.
